implementerProof.how: Each of the ten proofs in .legion/INFRA-264/implement.json was re-driven independently, not re-run from the implementer's rig: a second DPoP/RFC 8693 client written from RFC 9449 and RFC 8693 with the Go standard library alone (ES256 JWS, RFC 7638 thumbprint, jti/htm/htu/iat/ath), never internal/broker/helper, against the same live pair (packages/envoy/scripts/dev-broker.sh at http://127.0.0.1:65136 and packages/dispatch e2e/local-instance.ts at http://127.0.0.1:16410, both on the issue pod's own Postgres). Every status, code and message the handoff records was reproduced, and the broker-side tests it names were run against the real cmd/broker binary. Two things the handoff claims only by argument were driven as well and hold: the fifteen-second re-resolution of an open stream (a /ws/live socket under a broker token stayed open 45 s, three heartbeats, with two frames and no close) and that brokertoken.Presented does not eat a multipart body (a multipart artifact upload under a broker token answered 201). The eleventh proof the architect required (the dev box token half of the revocation line) is absent from the handoff and from the pull request body; it is recorded as a failure below, and the behaviour itself was driven here and holds.

failures.criterion: The change can be reviewed and merged: the base branch's required checks (lint, typecheck, test — pr-and-main.yaml, no path filter) run on the head under test.
failures.evidence: No workflow run has ever existed for this pull request. `gh run list --repo sjawhar/legion --branch legion/INFRA-264 --limit 30` prints nothing; `gh api repos/sjawhar/legion/commits/<sha>/check-runs` is empty at both the code head e9d7da2e8848f33dc4c9e3c97793975e7a966a2d and the pull request head e48e947fc0b69754d22d0e5da54c9be391726ed8; `gh pr checks 2541` answers 'no checks reported on the legion/INFRA-264 branch'; `gh api repos/sjawhar/legion/commits/e48e947f.../status` answers state=pending with 0 statuses. The cause is that the pull request conflicts with its base: `gh pr view 2541 --json mergeable,mergeStateStatus` answers mergeable=CONFLICTING, mergeStateStatus=DIRTY, and GitHub starts no run triggered `on: pull_request` at a head that conflicts (skill://legion-worker/references/skip-checks-trailer.md states this; pull_request is this branch's only trigger, since envoy-and-contracts.yaml and pr-and-main.yaml take push on main alone). The conflict is real and wide: main has moved 62 commits past the fork point 8a911ecca3a5, and seventeen files are changed on both sides, among them packages/envoy/internal/dispatch/api/{server.go,routes_table.go,issue_create.go}, internal/dispatch/docs/websocket.go, internal/dispatch/model/model.go, cmd/dispatch/main.go, packages/contracts/src/{dispatch-api.ts,dispatch-tools.ts} and packages/envoy-client/src/dispatch-execute.ts. So nothing static — lint, types, the Go and Bun suites, the private-name check in CI, the worker-image and docs lanes — has ever judged this change, a base that requires a check will not merge a head whose checks never ran, and a pull-request body edit re-triggers nothing here (the head also ends with the `skip-checks: true` trailer). Remedy: bring the base in on this real conflict (skill://legion-worker/references/conflicts-and-rewrites.md, 'Reintegrating the base'), push that head carrying no trailer so the required checks run, and keep the handoff-only push separate. The forward merge moves the unchanged-diff fingerprint, so a full test round follows it rather than a bare-gate re-check.
failures.redTest: none: this is the state of the branch on GitHub, not a behaviour a test in this repository can pin, and the deployment instructions forbid a test that reads a workflow file or checks a check.

failures.criterion: A revoked token stops working within the cache's few seconds, proven on the dev box token as well as on an exchanged one (INFRA-264; plan P14 as the architect amended it in dispatch://INFRA-264/comment/f968ddb6 point 4: 'The dev box token proof stays too').
failures.evidence: The implement handoff's ten proofs and the pull request body carry only the exchanged-token half (POST /v1/oauth/revoke, RFC 7009). Neither names a machine login, POST /v1/launcher-credentials/{id}/revoke-by-approver, or a token whose project_scope is person. The behaviour itself is sound — this phase drove it end to end (proof entry 'revocation, dev box token' below): a device-authorization machine login approved through agent-secrets-devrelay, its machine access token exchanged for session ada-devbox (introspection: project_scope person, no project), accepted at whoami, then revoked by approver, and Dispatch refused it at t=+5.2 s having accepted it at t=+4.7 s. What is missing is the implementer's own record of it, which the architect asked for by name; add the eleventh proof entry and the pull request body's matching clause. Note for whoever drives it next: `agent-secrets machine login` cannot run in this pod at all — the helper socket answers PEER_UNIDENTIFIED: SO_PEERPIDFD: protocol not available under gVisor — so the login has to be driven as the four HTTP steps (device_authorization with an RFC 9101 request object and dpop_jkt, devrelay machine-approve, the device_code redemption, then the token exchange with subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token).
failures.redTest: none: no behaviour is wrong, so there is nothing to pin red. What is missing is a recorded proof.

proof.criterion: A caller presenting a broker-issued token is accepted, and Dispatch reports the session, the person and the project (INFRA-264).
proof.surface: The live pair: packages/envoy/scripts/dev-broker.sh (real cmd/broker, real dev-oidc-issuer, its own Postgres database) and packages/dispatch `bun run dispatch:local` (real Go server, real Postgres, the production SPA build), driven by a second DPoP client written from the RFCs with the Go standard library alone.
proof.command: dpopdrv exchange --subject-token-file $DEV_BROKER_DIR/exchange-token --session example-worker-session; then GET http://127.0.0.1:16410/api/v1/whoami under 'Authorization: DPoP <token>' with a proof carrying jti/htm/htu/iat/ath
proof.observed: 200 {"kind":"agent","owner":"ada@example.com","project":"EXAMPLE","service":null,"session":"example-worker-session"} — every field from the token; the request carried no actor and no body.
proof.negativeControl: The same token under Bearer → 401 UNAUTHORIZED 'invalid bearer token'; under DPoP with no proof header → 401 BROKER_TOKEN_PROOF_INVALID; with the proof's ath removed → 401 BROKER_TOKEN_PROOF_INVALID; with an ath of another token → 401 BROKER_TOKEN_PROOF_INVALID; with htu naming another origin (http://evil.example/api/v1/whoami) → 401 BROKER_TOKEN_PROOF_INVALID; with typ jwt rather than dpop+jwt → 401 BROKER_TOKEN_PROOF_INVALID; one jti presented twice → the second 401 BROKER_TOKEN_PROOF_INVALID (the replay store); iat ten minutes either side of now → 401 BROKER_TOKEN_PROOF_INVALID. 'Authorization: dpop <token>' lower-cased is accepted, as the scheme is case-insensitive.

proof.criterion: A call whose actor names a session the token does not is refused (INFRA-264).
proof.surface: The same live pair: POST /api/v1/issues/EXAMPLE-1/comments with one broker token, varying the body's actor.
proof.command: POST /api/v1/issues/EXAMPLE-1/comments under DPoP four times: no actor; actor {kind session, id example-worker-session}; actor {kind session, id ses-not-mine}; actor {kind user, id alice}
proof.observed: No actor → 201, author {"kind":"session","id":"example-worker-session","owner":"ada@example.com","project":"EXAMPLE"}; the matching actor → 201 with the same author; another session → 403 ACTOR_SESSION_MISMATCH 'this request's credential acts for session example-worker-session; its actor names another writer'; a user actor → the same 403.
proof.negativeControl: The absent and matching actors both write in the same run, so the refusal is the mismatch and not the presence of an actor.

proof.criterion: A token whose key the caller cannot prove it holds is refused (INFRA-264).
proof.surface: The same live pair: GET /api/v1/whoami proved by a second ES256 key.
proof.command: dpopdrv request GET /api/v1/whoami --proof-key <a freshly generated P-256 key>, then the same request with the token's own key
proof.observed: The other key → 401 BROKER_TOKEN_KEY_MISMATCH 'the DPoP proof's key is not the key this access token is bound to'; the token's own key → 200 with the session, person and project.
proof.negativeControl: The accepted half above, in the same run, so the refusal is the key and not the token.

proof.criterion: A revoked token stops working within the cache's few seconds, and a refusal is never served from a cache — the exchanged-token half (INFRA-264, the architect's point 4).
proof.surface: The same live pair, with a counting reverse proxy between Dispatch and the broker so every introspection Dispatch makes is observable from outside Dispatch (Dispatch's DISPATCH_AGENT_SECRETS_URL pointed at it).
proof.command: whoami (caches the affirmative answer at t=0), then POST /v1/oauth/revoke at the broker as the dispatch caller (form token=<access token>&token_type_hint=access_token&client_id=dispatch-token-exchange), then whoami every half second
proof.observed: Accepted at t=+0.0 through +4.7 s, 401 BROKER_TOKEN_NOT_ACTIVE at t=+5.3 s — the five-second affirmative cache and no longer. The whole window cost two introspections, the cached one and the one that saw the revocation. A refusal is never cached: one unknown token presented twice cost two introspections and answered 401 BROKER_TOKEN_NOT_ACTIVE twice. The cache and its single flight were measured in the same way: five presentations of a fresh token within 1.5 s cost one introspection, a sixth after five seconds cost a second, and ten concurrent presentations of a fresh token cost exactly one introspection with all ten answered 200.
proof.negativeControl: The same revocation presented by the introspection-only caller → 403 ACCOUNT_LACKS_POWER 'the caller "listener" may not call POST /v1/oauth/revoke', and whoami stayed 200, so the refusal is the power and not the request.

proof.criterion: A revoked token stops working within the cache's few seconds — the dev box token half (INFRA-264; the architect's point 4, which the implement handoff does not carry).
proof.surface: The same live pair, driving a person's machine login by hand: POST /v1/oauth/device_authorization with an RFC 9101 request object (typ agent-secrets-request+jwt, launcher_credential detail, login_hint ada@example.com) and dpop_jkt, approved with agent-secrets-devrelay machine-approve, redeemed for the machine access token, then exchanged for a Dispatch token under session ada-devbox.
proof.command: POST /v1/oauth/token (token-exchange, subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token, session=ada-devbox); GET /api/v1/whoami; POST /v1/launcher-credentials/4f947816-2ad4-40be-8212-667e31780313/revoke-by-approver as the dispatch caller; then whoami every half second
proof.observed: Introspection: {"active":true,"session":"ada-devbox","person":"ada@example.com","project_scope":"person","client_id":"dispatch-token-exchange"} with no project. whoami → 200 {"kind":"agent","owner":"ada@example.com","project":null,"service":null,"session":"ada-devbox"}, and that token wrote both CORE-1 and EXAMPLE-1 (201 each), which is the documented rule: a person-scoped token carries no project and the project check is a no-op for it. The revoke answered {"state":"revoked"}; Dispatch accepted at t=+4.7 s and refused at t=+5.2 s with 401 BROKER_TOKEN_NOT_ACTIVE.
proof.negativeControl: The same revoke-by-approver presented by the introspection-only caller → 403 ACCOUNT_LACKS_POWER naming that caller and that route, with the token still accepted afterwards.

proof.criterion: The document editor's live connection no longer accepts a shared bearer, and a person's own connection still edits (INFRA-264).
proof.surface: The live Dispatch: GET /ws/doc/{document} upgraded three ways with curl --http1.1, and the repository's own browser suite in a real Chromium against the production SPA build.
proof.command: Upgrade /ws/doc/cd16858b-f577-44e9-a790-394cd460fc17 with 'Authorization: Bearer e2e-token' and the old X-Dispatch-Actor header; with a signed-in person's cookie; with a broker token under DPoP. Then `bunx playwright test --config e2e/playwright.config.ts --project=chromium e2e/doc.e2e.ts e2e/collab-cursor.e2e.ts` against the same instance.
proof.observed: The deployment's shared token → 401 Unauthorized; a broker token → 401 Unauthorized; the person's cookie → 101 Switching Protocols. The browser suite: 17 of 17 rows passed in 1.7 m, two people editing one document live, their cursors, named versions, the diff, an agent edit landing in an open editor, reconnection after a dropped transport. `grep -rn 'X-Dispatch-Actor'` over the tree finds the name in packages/envoy/CHANGELOG.md and nowhere else.
proof.negativeControl: The same shared token on the HTTP API in the same run → 200 at /api/v1/whoami, so the socket's 401 is the deleted door and not a wrong token.

proof.criterion: A write to an object of a project the token does not cover is refused and names both projects; the same call against its own project succeeds; a write that belongs to no project is refused to a project-scoped token (INFRA-265).
proof.surface: The same live pair, with two projects (EXAMPLE, which the token names, and the seed's CORE) and one object of every addressing kind in each.
proof.command: Under one EXAMPLE-scoped token: POST /api/v1/issues/{EXAMPLE-1,CORE-1}/comments; PATCH /api/v1/issues/CORE-1; POST /api/v1/comments/{a CORE comment}/reply; POST /api/v1/asks/{a CORE ask}/{resolve,answer}; POST /api/v1/artifacts/{a CORE document}/versions; POST /api/v1/projects/CORE/artifacts; POST /api/v1/issues with project CORE and with project EXAMPLE; POST /api/v1/projects; POST /api/v1/broadcasts
proof.observed: Its own project → 201 (a comment) and 201 (EXAMPLE-2, the issue create, whose project the body names). Every CORE address → 403 PROJECT_SCOPE 'this request's credential may write project EXAMPLE; this write belongs to project CORE', one for each of the issue-key, comment-id, ask-id, artifact-id and project-key kinds. POST /api/v1/projects → 403 PROJECT_SCOPE_DEPLOYMENT naming the route; POST /api/v1/broadcasts → the same. An id that names nothing (an unknown uuid, a non-uuid) is left to its handler and answers what it always answered, so the check never turns an unknown id into an answer about which projects exist.
proof.negativeControl: In the same run a signed-in person's cookie created both projects and their issues and held the document socket, and the shared token answered 200 at whoami: the check is a no-op for every credential that names no project. The route table's own walk carries the other direction — `go test ./internal/dispatch/api -run TestEveryMutatingRouteIsClassed` passes, and its two sub-tests are the negative control, failing on a fixture with an unclassed mutating row and on one classed as a project's write whose address names no object.

proof.criterion: A project-scoped token reaches nothing it should not through a route classed as the calling session's or the deployment's (INFRA-265, read as an attacker rather than as a table).
proof.surface: The same live pair: every scopeSession row a session caller can address, driven across sessions and projects.
proof.command: Under the EXAMPLE token: POST /api/v1/me/agent-tokens; POST /api/v1/agents/{another session}/messages; POST /api/v1/agents/{another session}/artifacts; PUT /api/v1/me/issues/CORE-1/state; POST /api/v1/messages/{a direct message}/reply
proof.observed: 403 HUMAN_ONLY for the personal-token mint, for a message into another session's conversation and for the user state; 400 ARTIFACT_INPUT for the conversation upload; 403 REPLY_FORBIDDEN for the delivery reply. No path from a project-scoped pod token to an unscoped credential or to another session's conversation.
proof.negativeControl: The same calls as the signed-in person succeed in the seed (the instance's own seeding makes them), so the refusals are the caller's standing and not a broken route.

proof.criterion: Dispatch's unauthenticated path cannot spend the people's approval budget (plan P5), and the broker is never asked twice for one answer.
proof.surface: The same live pair with the counting proxy between Dispatch and the broker.
proof.command: Forty presentations of forty distinct unknown tokens from one source address, counting the introspections that reached the broker
proof.observed: 31 reached the broker (31 × 401 BROKER_TOKEN_NOT_ACTIVE) and 9 were refused 401 BROKER_TOKEN_RATE_LIMITED without the broker being asked at all; the bound is the per-source-address bucket, spent inside the single flight.
proof.negativeControl: The honest caller in the same stack is unaffected: ten concurrent presentations of one live token cost one introspection and all ten answered 200.

proof.criterion: A broker outage refuses a broker-token caller rather than quietly unscoping it (the project check reads the caller itself, so this is where it could fail open).
proof.surface: The same live pair with the broker stopped.
proof.command: With cmd/broker killed: GET /api/v1/whoami; POST /api/v1/issues/EXAMPLE-1/comments; POST /api/v1/issues/CORE-1/comments; POST /api/v1/projects — all under a token minted before the outage
proof.observed: 503 BROKER_UNAVAILABLE 'the secrets broker cannot be reached; try again in a minute' on every one, the write to its own project included, so no write runs unscoped while the broker is down.
proof.negativeControl: In the same outage the shared token and a person's cookie both answered 200 at /api/v1/whoami, so the 503 is the broker-token branch alone.

proof.criterion: A pod cannot obtain a token naming a session of another issue, a relaunch is never refused, and a fixed-session account survives a rollout (INFRA-382).
proof.surface: The real cmd/broker binary against a real Postgres, and the live dev stack.
proof.command: BROKER_TEST_DATABASE_URL=… go test -count=1 -run TestAPodWritesOnlyUnderASessionRegisteredForIt -v ./cmd/broker; and go test -tags multiprocess -count=1 -run TestAFixedSessionNameAcrossARollout -v ./cmd/broker
proof.observed: Both pass. The registered pod exchanges (200); a second pod uid of the same account registered for the same name — the relaunch — exchanges too; an unregistered third pod uid is 400 invalid_grant 'No registration says this pod may write under the session name …. A pod writes under a session name its deployment registered for it'; registering that third pod answers it. The rollout test's four parts pass, including a fixed-session entry whose pods need no registration and the stranger refused the fixed name. The live stack showed the same refusal by hand.
proof.negativeControl: The identical request naming the session the dev script registered for that pod mints a token in the same run. The real-pod relaunch stays with dispatch://INFRA-267 by the architect's ruling (dispatch://INFRA-264/comment/f968ddb6 point 1).

proof.criterion: The pull request body states exactly what the session binding holds and what it does not (INFRA-382).
proof.surface: The pull request body's section 'What the session binding holds, and what it does not (INFRA-382)' read against the code it describes.
proof.command: Each of its five sentences read against packages/envoy/internal/broker/exchange/exchange.go:295-330 and packages/envoy/internal/broker/oauthstore/exchange.go:49-63
proof.observed: All five hold: the principal is the account (accountPrincipal at :323, so a registered successor keeps the name); Instance is set only for an entry that fixes no session (:325-327), so the registration is the only thing separating two pods of one account; a fixed entry answers no Instance and needs none (:304-306); the token is verified offline, so the broker asks the cluster nothing (:295-296); PodSessionRetention is 24 hours from each write (oauthstore/exchange.go:63), which is the window a daemon that stops registering costs its pods.
proof.negativeControl: The claim the body does not make is the one the code does not support: nothing there says a deleted pod's token stops working, and the code shows it does not.

proof.criterion: An account listed only for introspection is refused approve, deny and both revokes by name, and listing a second account cannot silently widen the first (INFRA-401).
proof.surface: The real cmd/broker binary with two listed accounts, and the live dev stack's two callers.
proof.command: BROKER_TEST_DATABASE_URL=… go test -count=1 -run TestAListedAccountReachesOnlyItsOwnRoutes -v ./cmd/broker; go test -run TestEveryAccountRouteDeclaresItsPower -v ./internal/broker/api; and by hand against the live broker as the listener token
proof.observed: Twenty-two subtests pass: the listener caller is 403 ACCOUNT_LACKS_POWER on every relay route, naming itself and the route, reaches introspection, and the dispatch caller reaches all eleven. By hand the listener token was refused POST /v1/oauth/revoke and POST /v1/launcher-credentials/{id}/revoke-by-approver with the same code and message while the dispatch token carried both out. Every accountAuth row declares a power (eleven subtests).
proof.negativeControl: TestEveryAccountRouteDeclaresItsPower fails on a row that declares none and api.Register refuses to mount such a table; a caller name BROKER_API_ACCOUNTS gives that the broker does not know refuses the boot.

proof.surface: The broker's own account-authenticated routes with a counting test issuer, and the oidc package's suite.
proof.observed: All pass: TestAForgedAccountTokenFloodFromManyAddressesCostsOneFetchPerMinute, TestOneAddressFloodingItsLimitLeavesOthersTheirRereads (the legitimate caller during the flood), TestAForgedAccountTokenFloodIsLimitedByAddress and TestAForgedAccountTokenFloodStopsReachingTheVerifier, and the oidc suite with the rotation and the issuer-unavailable classes.

environment.note: The issue pod has no Docker, no root and no Postgres of its own; the harness is the unpacked-Debian Postgres 17 the implementer left at /legion/harness (docs/solutions/testing/the-real-dispatch-stack-runs-inside-a-legion-pod-with-no-postgres-no-docker-and-no-root-INFRA-42.md). Two pod limits bear on what can be driven here, neither a defect of this change: gVisor answers SO_PEERPIDFD 'protocol not available', so agent-secrets-helper refuses every local client (PEER_UNIDENTIFIED) and a machine login has to be driven as its four HTTP steps; and playwright's webkit and firefox cannot be installed, so only chromium rows run.
